arc: The teaching first surveys the structural scaffolding of the cosmos — pillars, firmaments, angels, the encircling sea, the Omophoros bearing up the worlds — and then turns to ask what the liturgical "Yes" and "Amen" mean, answering that they are nothing other than the Call and the Hearing, the very principles by which the First Man was raised and by which the Living Soul is now refined.
title: The Yes and the Amen: cosmic scaffolding revealed as the Call and the Hearing
reading:
The teaching has two movements that belong together. The first half catalogues the architecture of the cosmos as a built thing — the seven pillars that stand, the sea that encircles the cosmos, the four angels stretched forth and bearing up the world under the strength of the divine, the earth and all the heavens below, the twelve angels and twenty-two angels disposed in their orders, the twelve likenesses, the three great pillars of strength, the firmaments which the Spirit has placed at that very hour, the great Omophoros holding the cosmos in his power. Within this scaffolding stand the figures who keep the work alive: Adamas of Light, the Youth (Jesus the Radiance) beneath, and the "other five gods, food of the man" — the Five Sons of the First Man as the Living Soul nourishing the cosmic-man. The whole built order is presented as one structure, and the burden of the description is that "the cosmos stands fast at the Calling." The structure is not self-supporting; it holds because a summons holds it.

That sentence is the hinge. The second half of the teaching opens with a request to add a name in blessing alongside the Blessed One, and with the question: "Tell us, what is the Yes and the Amen?" The answer is the heart of the chapter. The Yes and the Amen have come into being from the great ones of the powers and were given a name: the Yes is reckoned to the Calling, the Amen to the Answer — that is, to the Hearing. They are those who opened their mouths to the Spirit and to the petitioning before the First Man. They are not themselves the high reigning ones of the Father of Life and the Mother of Life, not the Aromaios who came forth through them — that is, the First Man himself; rather, the Calling and the Hearing are those who have reigned for them, the active agents through whom the lordship of the high powers is exercised in the cosmic-arena.

So the teaching identifies the liturgical "Yes" and "Amen" with the two great cosmic operations of redemption. The Calling is Divine Truth's summons reaching downward into mingling and Death; the Hearing is the Living Soul's response rising back upward. These two are what reigned through all the Aeons of lordship until the moment when the First Man, with the soul mingled with Death, needed to be raised. They were his helpers in his ascent; they gave him over to the Father of the Living One and the Mother of Life. And what they did once for the First Man they continue to do now: they are the refiners of the Living Soul, helpers and givers to her of the Remembrance — whether in the tree (in the perception that grows and bears fruit) or in the fashioning of the flesh (in the very molding of bodily life). Wherever the Living Soul is dispersed, the Calling reaches her and the Hearing returns her.

The two halves of the teaching therefore say one thing. The pillars, firmaments, four bearing-angels, Omophoros and the three great columns of strength are not merely a cosmography; they are the standing apparatus through which the Calling descends and the Hearing rises. The cosmos "stands fast at the Calling" because the Call is what holds the structure open for redemption, and the Amen-Hearing is what closes the circuit. When a believer says "Yes" and "Amen" in prayer, those words are not mere assent: they are participation in the same two principles that raised the First Man and that daily refine the Living Soul through tree and flesh. The fragmentary state of the surviving text obscures details of the angelic counts and of the third great pillar's function, but the whole arc is clear — from the built cosmos to the liturgical word, and from the liturgical word back to the cosmic mechanism of redemption.
